en: Hymn of Praise for the Descent of Śākyamuni (with Preface) Composed by the Śramaṇa Renyue of Xixi The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"From the day of the Buddha’s birth until the day of his parinirvāṇa, one should extol the virtues of the Buddha before the great assembly."
In my youth, I read the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra and extracted the signs of the Teacher’s manifestation of passing away at the Twin Śāla Trees, composing verses to give voice to them.

Recently, there were those among our own school who took an interest in this matter and requested that on the eighth day of the fourth month, during the ceremony of bathing the Buddha image, I also present hymns of praise.
This was so that the ritual procedures of the *Mahāsāṃghika* could be fully prepared from beginning to end. Thereupon, I investigated the accounts of the Prince’s origins and his causal history.
The categories of events described in the *Phala-sūtra* and other scriptures are briefly praised as tenfold, followed by the sequence of the five methods of repentance.

Originally, the manner in which the Tathāgata responds to sentient beings varies according to their capacities; thus, his entry into the womb riding a white elephant and his descent of the consciousness (*vijñāna*) while presiding over a fragrant tower cannot be considered identical.
Now, relying on the teachings of the Hīnayāna, we shall take up his conduct prior to the Deer Park.

The matters concerning the causes, destinies, and fruits have been composed into chapters and verses. As for the traces of transformation throughout the five periods, these do not fully encompass the Way;
yet, if one dares to speak of them with reckless artistry, I shall attempt to arrange them here.

(The assembly of monks gathers at the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*). First, they pay homage to the Triple Gem. Next, they bathe the Buddha image. Then, kneeling alternately, they burn incense, each reciting verses which are appended at the end of this volume).

Now, among the three luminaries that illuminate the world, none is more magnificent than the solar disc; among the four types of noble beings who transform others, none is more honored than the Buddha-way.
Yet, because the Great Illumination is easily accessible, true awakening is difficult to encounter. Thus, as the long night grows ever darker, the myriad living beings fail to attain realization.

Alas, since the virtuous *kalpa* has declined and the turbid, evil realms have increased, we find ourselves in this world of endurance (*sahā*) without a teacher, meeting only those who are capable...

A Confucian who has transcended the world, manifesting as a member of the Kṣatriya caste yet not acting as a king over the seven treasures; having realized Bodhi, he thus became the Lord of the Thousand Flowers.

His form and voice respond to things, and his excellence or inferiority accords with the capacities of beings. Although the ritual manifestations of his transformation have a beginning and an end, the True Dharma is fundamentally without coming or going.
Now, coinciding with the third month of spring, the anniversary of the eight phases of his birth, we recall his past...

For this cause and condition, I venture to offer praise and verse, providing seasonal offerings as a modest expression of my diligent sincerity. I pray that your holy compassion will look down upon me with clear discernment.
With a single mind, I reverently invoke Śākyamuni Buddha, who manifested his birth in the Sahā World.
I pray that you will descend to this site of practice and accept my offerings.
In the heavens above and the earth below, none is like the Buddha; Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is no equal.
I have seen all that exists within the world, And among them, none is like the Buddha.

(At this point, either a formal narrative is recited or the text of the memorial is proclaimed—such as addressing the Buddha—as determined by the occasion. Thereafter, perform prostrations and praises, chanting:
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to Śākyamuni Buddha, who was prophesied by Dīpaṃkara Buddha when he was the Bodhisattva. (The following cases shall follow this example.)
In the distant past, while practicing the bodhisattva path, he encountered a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara.
Having been a young brahmin (maṇava), he offered compassion; because of this, he made offerings with Gopī.
He spread his hair to cover the mud beneath the Buddha’s feet, and scattered flowers that formed a canopy suspended in mid-air.

From this point on, having attained the dharma-patience of non-arising and having personally received the prediction of Śākyamuni Buddha, I single-mindedly take refuge in and pay homage to [him]. (The following cases shall follow this pattern.)

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the one who manifests in the Tuṣita Heaven as a Bodhisattva in his final birth, destined to realize the fruit of the Able One (Śākyamuni) in this very life;

From that state of final rebirth, he ascends to the Heaven of Joy (Tuṣita), having transcended the realm of desire to dwell in the celestial abodes; There, for the sake of weary beings, he expounds the True Dharma.
The kalpa-fire cannot burn this realm; the light from a single pore still illuminates all the dhyāna heavens.
Awaiting the ripening of conditions, he descends to be born, universally causing those in blindness and darkness to open their eyes of wisdom.
With one mind, I prostrate to the body of the mother Māyā while she was pregnant in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
Entrusting his consciousness to the Queen, he was named Mahāmāyā; His radiant light reached Kapilavastu within India, responding to a dream with a hidden communication of the jade-elephant form.
Abiding in the womb, he was truly of the lineage of the Golden Wheel-turning King;
In the tenth month, he proclaimed the subtle teachings through his voice, While the various devas first beheld his marks adorning his body.
Within this Benevolent and Worthy Kalpa, the great void is vast; now we shall celebrate the rare appearance of the *tánhuá* flower.
With a single mind, I prostrate before the body of the Queen who gave birth beneath the Ashoka tree, from her right side.
When the Holy Queen entered the garden and climbed a tree, she gave birth with ease from her right side to a golden body.
Having taken seven steps, he manifested extraordinary auspicious signs; pointing toward the two realms of heaven and earth, he declared himself the most supreme.
Heaven rained down fine incense that moistened all things, and the earth opened to reveal hidden treasures, all of them brilliant and pure.
Reverently pay homage to the centenarian Āyu, who prophesied that you, with your marks and signs, shall become a Buddha;
to the one who single-mindedly prostrated at the Eastern Palace upon receiving his office, and who manifested the body of one who had taken a consort yet grew weary of desire.
The Crown Prince, in the prime of his youth, pursued learning; His father the King sought a bride and obtained Yaśodharā.
Though the five desires constantly enticed him, He saw only that his faculties were ever tranquil.
A lotus born from turbid water is pure at its core; Gold in a red furnace remains unchanged in essence.
In vain did she increase her beauty and follow him constantly; in the end, he was severed from the net of craving by the sword of wisdom.
With single-minded devotion, he prostrated himself and wandered through the four gates, beholding impermanence and delighting in the path of liberation.
He solemnly mounted his carriage and traveled through the four gates to observe the four signs; The sons of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven transformed various appearances for him.
First encountering old age and decay, he sighed at impermanence; Later seeing a true monk, he rejoiced in the existence of the Way.
How could the Sage’s intent have been to pursue worldly pleasures? Only empty sounds praised the conditions for transcending the mundane.
Having pledged through the joining of palms to remain pregnant so as to provide an heir for the Father King, she focused her mind solely on awaiting the departure from the palace;
with single-minded devotion, she prostrated before the Crown Prince at midnight, crossing the city walls to leave the world in that very body.
The Celestial One spoke: "The time for renunciation has arrived. He then abandoned the royal kingdom and pointed toward a mountain;
at midnight, the palace gates opened of their own accord. The divine colt of a thousand *li* galloped away in an instant;
Chandaka returned to the palace, lost on the distant road. Yaśodharā, carrying her child, remained by the empty curtains.
The ten-thousand chariots followed in pursuit but ultimately did not turn back;
instead, they were moved to gaze from afar and pay homage with single-minded devotion to the body that had practiced austerities for six years within Gayāśīrṣa Mountain.
The five attendants all desisted midway; for six years he practiced cultivation while seeking it abroad.
On the Snowy Range, there was no spring, and he endured bitter cold; though his rosy countenance had not yet aged, he grew equally withered.
Filling his hunger with hemp and wheat, how could this be the Way? Severing [extremes] and practicing fixed concentration—this too is not the truth.
This was an expedient means to transform sentient beings, gradually leading those of heterodox ways to return to perfect enlightenment;
with a single mind, I prostrate at the body of the Buddha when he received alms-food from Nanda on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River.
The Great Power-Holder shall receive offerings from humans and devas; First he accepted the milk-gruel offered by Nanda.
Though the Bodhisattva sustained his wondrous physical body, How could Vairocana have required the flavor of rare delicacies?
Having shaved his hair, he returned to the Lord of Trāyastriṃśa; The transmission of the robe originally came from the Master Kāśyapa.
Walking, I behold the Bodhi tree drawing near; with every step, the earth and its carriage tremble.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate before the body that sat upon the Vajra-seat, having subdued the celestial Māras at the moment of attaining enlightenment.
Sitting cross-legged upon a bed of grass through the long night, when the thirty-four minds were fully perfected,
the defilements of the nine stages were severed and eliminated, and the demonic affairs of the six heavens were all subdued.
Great Brahmā awaited to hear the drum of nectar, while the multitudes of living beings came to behold the Purple Gold Mountain.
Thus, by turning the Wheel of Dharma according to what is appropriate, all people have received its grace to this very day.
(At this point, kneel again; holding the incense burner and directing the mind, recite the Five Repentances.)
With a sincere heart, we repent:
since the time we first possessed consciousness, we have followed along with ignorance, dwelling in evil realms for a vast duration and turning upon the wheel of suffering at its will.

Although a Buddha has arisen in this Sahā world, we have not encountered the Honored One of Ten Thousand Virtues; although the Dharma covers all weary beings, we have been unable to receive even a single sound of his teaching.

This teaching is truly because the roots of transgression are deep-seated and firm, while the seeds of goodness are faint and obscure. It is not that the response of the Transformation Body is partial;

rather, it is the karmic conditions that act as an obstruction. We still rely upon the *Pāli* scriptures brought from the West and the parable of the raft flowing to the East, so that we may hear of our Buddha’s descent into this world.
It is as if we have met him at that very moment to take refuge. Grief and joy converge, and shame and remorse increase all the more. Now, before this sacred site, I stand.
Therefore, I extend this repentance.
Having repented, I take refuge in the Triple Gem with a sincere heart (the remainder follows this pattern).
With a sincere heart, I entreat [the Buddhas].

I reverently invite all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm. Whether born in lands of the five turbidities, you shall preach the Way of the Three Vehicles;
may the clouds of wisdom cover all, and the rain of Dharma fall upon it, so that all living beings may be fully nourished and moistened.
With a sincere heart,
I rejoice in all mundane and supramundane roots of goodness, whether they be the true vehicle of the untainted or the accumulations of merit consisting of conditioned phenomena;
I rejoice in them all, making no distinction between enemies and kin, and aspiring that in the future we may meet upon the level ground of equality.
With a sincere heart,
I dedicate this slight portion of the merit from extolling the Tathāgata, dedicating it entirely toward the ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the adornment of the fruit of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, I hope that all the manifold virtues accumulated over many lifetimes may be bestowed universally upon all sentient beings without exception, so that together we may realize the true path.
With a sincere heart, I make this vow:

from my state as an ordinary being until I reach sainthood, throughout this world and all other realms, wherever a Buddha dwells, may I everywhere behold his manifestations of descending to appear in the world.
Upon first hearing his voice and teachings, may I immediately enter the Mahāyāna; and without delay, emerging from the weariness of worldly toil, may I ascend to the further shore.
(Circumambulate the maṇḍala clockwise. Recite the name of Śākyamuni Buddha, or chant the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct. Retire with utmost sincerity.
The Text for Prostrating and Praising upon the Birth of Śākyamuni (End).
Ritual for Bathing the Image of the Buddha.
According to the *Bathing the Image Sūtra* (*Yuxiang Gongde Jing*), the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, how should sentient beings in future ages bathe the images? The Buddha replied:
"One should use ox-head sandalwood, *tamaraka* incense, spikenard, *kunkuma*, saffron, camphor, aloeswood, musk, and clove. With these various kinds..."
Take various kinds of exquisite incense and, according to what is obtained, prepare a bath-water. Place it in a clean vessel and bathe the image in succession with these various fragrant waters.

After bathing it thus, wash the image again with pure water. Those who bathe in this manner should each take a small amount of the water used for washing the image and place it upon their own heads. Thereafter, they should burn various kinds of incense as an offering.
Gāthā for Bathing the Buddha:
I now bathe all the Tathāgatas, The assembly adorned with the merit of pure wisdom.
May the sentient beings of the five turbidities be freed from defilement, And may they realize the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Gatha for Burning Incense:
The incense of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation pervades the lands of the ten directions, remaining perpetually fragrant.
May this incense smoke likewise become so, transforming into the five bodies for both myself and others.
